title: A Dockerfile that works, and why that is the problem
summary: Build a Node.js app from a typical first Dockerfile. It runs fine, but it floats on "latest" and ships a secret. Find both, then fix them.

steps.text: Go to your home folder, make a folder for this track, and move into it. Every Node take-home exercise uses it.
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir takehome-node
cd takehome-node
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Create package.json. express runs the app. prettier is a development-only tool, which matters in the last exercise.
steps.label: package.json

steps.text: Create server.js. It answers with a greeting, and says whether it can see an API key.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Create a Dockerfile the way many first attempts look. It builds and runs, so nothing warns you about the two mistakes in it.
steps.code:
FROM node:latest
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
ENV API_KEY=sk-live-123
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

notes.text: Save it as Dockerfile, not Dockerfile.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Build and run it, then open http://localhost:8084. The first build downloads the full node image, which is large.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-shop .
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Mistake one: "latest" is whatever version was newest on the day you built. Check which Node you got and how big the image is. A teammate who builds next month can get a different major version from the same Dockerfile.
steps.code:
docker run --rm node-shop node --version
docker image ls node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Mistake two: the key. ENV values are saved in the image, so anyone who pulls it can read them. The build output even warned you: SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv.
steps.code:
docker history node-shop
docker image inspect node-shop --format '{{.Config.Env}}'
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Fix both. Pin a small, specific base image, and delete the ENV line.
steps.code:
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

steps.text: Rebuild and start it again, this time passing the key in with -e when the container starts. The page still says hasKey: true, but the image history no longer has the key, and the image is several hundred MB smaller.
steps.code:
docker rm -f node-shop
docker build -t node-shop .
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 -e API_KEY=sk-live-123 node-shop
docker history node-shop
docker image ls node-shop
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: A value passed with -e is not in the image you push, but anyone who can run docker inspect on that server can still read it. On a real server, keep secrets in an env file only the deploy user can read, or in your platform's secret store.

steps.text: Remove the container. You keep the folder and the image for the next exercise.
steps.code: docker rm -f node-shop
steps.label: terminal

expected: The first image lists ENV API_KEY=sk-live-123 in docker history. The rebuilt one does not, is much smaller, and the page at localhost:8084 still shows "hasKey": true.

files.note: Run every command from inside takehome-node.

entries.note: your working folder for the whole track

title: Stop cleanly
summary: docker stop asks your app to finish up, and Node ignores the request by default. Handle the signal so your app shuts down on time.

steps.text: Start the app again from the image you built.
steps.code: docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Stop it and watch how long it takes, then check how it ended. docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits a few seconds, and then kills the container. Exit code 137 means it was killed.
steps.code:
docker stop node-shop
docker ps -a --filter name=node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Why: in a container your app is process number 1, and Linux does not apply the usual "exit on SIGTERM" to process 1. Node only stops if the code asks it to. A killed app cannot finish requests or close its database connections. Add a handler to server.js.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Rebuild and run it, then open http://localhost:8084 so you know it has started.
steps.code:
docker rm node-shop
docker build -t node-shop .
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Stop it again. This time it stops at once, with exit code 0, and the log ends with "Stopping".
steps.code:
docker stop node-shop
docker ps -a --filter name=node-shop
docker logs node-shop
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: For an app you cannot change, docker run --init (or init: true in Compose) puts a tiny process 1 in front of it that passes the signal on. Also write CMD in the ["node", "server.js"] form: the plain CMD node server.js form can leave a shell as process 1, and shells do not pass the signal on either.

steps.text: Remove the container.
steps.code: docker rm node-shop
steps.label: terminal

expected: Before the fix: Exited (137) after a pause. After the fix: Exited (0) straight away, and "Stopping" at the end of docker logs.

title: Who can reach your app
summary: An app listening on 127.0.0.1 inside a container cannot be reached, even with -p. And a published port can be reached by more people than you think.

steps.text: Many dev servers listen on 127.0.0.1 by default. Make yours do the same: add '127.0.0.1' to app.listen.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Rebuild and run it. The log says "Listening on port 3000", yet http://localhost:8084 fails with an empty or reset response.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-shop .
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 node-shop
docker logs node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Why: inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container itself. Traffic from -p arrives on the container's network address instead, where nothing is listening. Listen on 0.0.0.0, which means every address.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Rebuild and run. Now localhost:8084 works.
steps.code:
docker rm -f node-shop
docker build -t node-shop .
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 8084:3000 node-shop
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: The other side: -p 8084:3000 opens 8084 on every network your machine is on, so anyone on the same Wi-Fi can reach it. On a Linux server it is worse: Docker writes its own firewall rules, so ufw or firewalld do not block a published port. That is how exposed databases get found and wiped. Publish to your own machine only by putting 127.0.0.1 in front. docker ps then shows 127.0.0.1:8084->3000.
steps.code:
docker rm -f node-shop
docker run -d --name node-shop -p 127.0.0.1:8084:3000 node-shop
docker ps --filter name=node-shop
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: A database almost never needs a published port. Other containers reach it over the Compose network by service name. Leave ports out of the db service entirely.

steps.text: Remove the container.
steps.code: docker rm -f node-shop
steps.label: terminal

expected: With 127.0.0.1 in app.listen the page does not load. With 0.0.0.0 it does, and docker ps shows 127.0.0.1:8084->3000/tcp for the last container.

title: Edit code without rebuilding
summary: A bind mount puts your folder inside the container, so edits show up at once. It can also hide what the image installed there.

steps.text: Create compose.yaml for development. The volumes line mounts this folder over /app in the container, and node --watch restarts the app when a file changes.
steps.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: ["node", "--watch", "server.js"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8084:3000"
    volumes:
      - ./:/app
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start it and read the log. The app crashes: Cannot find package 'express'.
steps.code:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs app
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Why: the image installed express into /app/node_modules, and the bind mount laid your folder over the whole of /app. Your folder has no node_modules, so the container no longer does either. Add a second volume line for /app/node_modules. It keeps the image's copy visible.
steps.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    command: ["node", "--watch", "server.js"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8084:3000"
    volumes:
      - ./:/app
      - /app/node_modules
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start it again and open http://localhost:8084. It works.
steps.code:
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs app
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Now change "Hello" to "Hi" in server.js and save.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Refresh the page. The change shows without a rebuild, because the container reads your file directly.

Remember the catch: /app/node_modules is now a volume that Compose keeps. After you change package.json, rebuild and ask for fresh volumes with -V, or the old packages stay. Stop it when you are done.
steps.code: docker compose down
steps.label: terminal

expected: First start: Cannot find package 'express' in the log. With the /app/node_modules line: the page loads, and changing "Hello" to "Hi" shows up after a refresh, with "Restarting 'server.js'" in the log.

files.note: Still inside takehome-node. Compose looks for compose.yaml in the current folder.

entries.note: step 1, one line added in step 3

title: Wait for the database
summary: Connect the app to Postgres with Compose. Meet two classic crashes, localhost and a database that is not ready yet, and make the stack come back after a crash.

steps.text: Add the Postgres client to package.json.
steps.label: package.json

steps.text: Replace server.js. It connects to the database when it starts, and shows the database's time.
steps.label: server.js

steps.text: Replace compose.yaml. The app finds the database through PGHOST, and depends_on starts db first.
steps.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: shop
    volumes:
      - shopdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      PGHOST: localhost
      PGUSER: postgres
      PGPASSWORD: shop
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8084:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db

volumes:
  shopdata:
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start it.
steps.code: docker compose up -d --build
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Give it a few seconds, then check. The app has exited, and its log says ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432. localhost inside the app container is the app container, and there is no database in it.
steps.code:
docker compose ps -a
docker compose logs app
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Point PGHOST at the service name instead. Compose gives every service a DNS name on the stack's network.
steps.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: shop
    volumes:
      - shopdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      PGHOST: db
      PGUSER: postgres
      PGPASSWORD: shop
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8084:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db

volumes:
  shopdata:
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start from scratch, as a fresh server would. This deletes the shopdata volume, which only holds an empty database here. The app crashes again, this time because Postgres was still setting itself up when the app tried to connect. depends_on only waits for the db container to start, not for the database to be ready.
steps.code:
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Give it a few seconds, then read the app's log. This time the name worked: the error shows the db container's address, or says the database system is starting up. Postgres just was not ready yet.
steps.code:
docker compose ps -a
docker compose logs app
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: If it happened to connect, run the last two steps again. It is a race, and a new database usually loses it.

steps.text: Fix it properly. The healthcheck asks Postgres whether it accepts connections, and condition: service_healthy makes the app wait for that. restart: unless-stopped brings a container back after a crash or a reboot. The logging limits stop the log file from growing until the disk is full.
steps.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: shop
    volumes:
      - shopdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-h", "127.0.0.1", "-U", "postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      retries: 15
    restart: unless-stopped

  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      PGHOST: db
      PGUSER: postgres
      PGPASSWORD: shop
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8084:3000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging:
      options:
        max-size: "10m"
        max-file: "3"

volumes:
  shopdata:
steps.label: compose.yaml

steps.text: Start from scratch again. This time db shows (healthy) before the app starts, and http://localhost:8084 shows the database's time.
steps.code:
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs app
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Crash the app on purpose, then check again. The restart policy starts it again within seconds.
steps.code:
docker compose exec app kill 1
docker compose ps
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Stop the stack. Plain down keeps the shopdata volume.
steps.code: docker compose down
steps.label: terminal

expected: Two failures first: ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432, then a failure on the db container's own address while Postgres was still starting. With the healthcheck: db (healthy), the app connected, the page shows databaseTime, and after kill 1 the app is Up again.

title: Build for the server's CPU
summary: An image is built for one kind of processor. Build on an Apple Silicon Mac and deploy to a normal server, and it will not start.

steps.text: Build the image and ask which CPU it is for. On an Apple Silicon Mac it says arm64. On most Windows and Intel machines it says amd64.
steps.code:
docker build -t node-shop .
docker image inspect node-shop --format '{{.Architecture}}'
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Most servers are amd64. An arm64 image fails there with "exec format error", and nothing else in the message says why. Build for the server's CPU with --platform.
steps.code:
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t node-shop:amd64 .
docker image inspect node-shop:amd64 --format '{{.Architecture}}'
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: On Apple Silicon this build runs under emulation, so it is slower. That is normal.

steps.text: Docker Desktop can even run the other CPU's image, by emulating it. Node reports x64, which is amd64. A plain Linux server cannot do this unless someone set emulation up.
steps.code: docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 node-shop:amd64 node -p process.arch
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: The safest habit: build release images in CI or on the server itself. docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 builds both at once, but has to push the result to a registry.

steps.text: Remove the extra image.
steps.code: docker image rm node-shop:amd64
steps.label: terminal

expected: Your own architecture first (arm64 or amd64), then amd64 for node-shop:amd64, and x64 from node -p process.arch.

title: Capstone: a Dockerfile fit for production
summary: Put it all together. Fix the rest of the Dockerfile yourself, compare with a worked answer, then clean up the whole track.

steps.text: Your Dockerfile is pinned and has no secret, but three mistakes from the course are still in it. Before you read on, try to name them and fix them yourself. Hints: a code change reinstalls every package; prettier ends up in the image; and the app runs as root.
Here is one answer. First, a .dockerignore, so node_modules, secrets and git history never reach the build.
steps.code:
node_modules
.env
.git
*.log
steps.label: .dockerignore

notes.text: Save it as .dockerignore, not .dockerignore.txt (choose "All files" in Notepad), or use VS Code.

steps.text: Then the Dockerfile: dependencies first so they are cached, --omit=dev to leave prettier out, NODE_ENV=production, and USER node so the app does not run as root. This app has no build step, so it needs only one stage. An app with a build step (TypeScript, Vite) builds in one stage and copies the result into a clean final one, as in the course's multi-stage exercise.
steps.code:
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production

# Dependencies first, so a code change does not reinstall them.
COPY package.json ./
RUN npm install --omit=dev

COPY . .
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
steps.label: Dockerfile

steps.text: Start the stack with the new image. The page at http://localhost:8084 works as before, whoami answers node, and prettier is not in the image.
steps.code:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose exec app whoami
docker compose exec app ls node_modules/prettier
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Check what the track cost in disk space. Images, build cache, volumes and logs all add up quietly on a server.
steps.code: docker system df
steps.label: terminal

steps.text: Clean up the whole track. This deletes the shopdata volume and its data for good, and removes the track's images.
steps.code:
docker compose down -v --rmi local
docker image rm node-shop
steps.label: terminal

notes.text: The large node:latest from the first exercise is still in the build cache. docker builder prune clears the cache, and docker system prune also clears stopped containers, unused networks and dangling images. Both delete permanently, so read what they list before you say yes.

steps.text: Delete the takehome-node folder when you no longer need it.

expected: whoami prints node, ls node_modules/prettier fails with "No such file or directory", and the page still shows databaseTime. After the cleanup, docker system df shows less in use.
